items.title: Good Secrets on Crafting a Bold Visual Identity for HBO’s 'U.S. Against the World'
items.summary: For animation and design studio Good Secrets, finding the visual language of a project always starts with understanding the heart of the story. On the HBO docuseries U.S. Against the World, that meant creating a bold, handcrafted visual identity that matched the grit, swagger, and emotional intensity of the U.S. Men’s National Soccer Team in the lead-up to the 2026 World Cup. Working closely with the series creators, Good Secrets developed a dynamic title sequence and graphics package that helped anchor the docuseries' non-linear narrative, seamlessly blending archival treatments, scorecards, maps, and animated sequences into a cohesive visual world. The team grounded their workflow in a scalable design system with Adobe After Effects, Essential Graphics, and Motion Graphics Templates (MOGRTs), ensuring their assets could evolve alongside an edit that was constantly changing. We spoke with Creative Director Casey Latiolais about building the show's distinctive aesthetic, balancing creativity with the demands of a five-hour docuseries, and why sometimes the best design starts with scissors, paper, and spray paint. How did you begin the design process for U.S. Against the World? Casey Latiolais: We got involved because we liked the story and knew the show was going to be good. We were also handed a huge canvas, and that's an offer you can’t turn down. We coordinated closely with the post-house so our graphics dropped into their pipeline without friction. Episodes and segments kept changing right up to the end, so we built for change. Templates for everything, sorted into categories: archival treatments, scorecards, locations, maps, etc. With a non-linear story, there's a lot of jumping around. Our job was keeping the viewer grounded through all of it. What conversations did you have with the wider team to align on the creative vision for the project? items.title: This New Steadicam Stabilizer Sled Brings Smarter Design and a Wider Range of Controls
items.summary: Steadicam has introduced its new Elite Stabilizer Sled, designed for broadcast applications and set to feature a smarter design and a much wider range of integrated controls. A familiar name in the Steadicam business, Steadicam certainly knows its technology and niche very well. So when Steadicam drops a new, you know, steadicam, you know it’s going to be a top option for those looking for a trusted level of sophisticated stabilization. And that’s what the new Elite Stabilizer Sled from Steadicam appears to offer as a lightweight stabilization system for broadcast applications, set to feature a smarter design and a wide variety of integrated controls. Let’s look into it. Steadicam Elite Stabilizer Sled While it’s being marketed for broadcast applications, this new Elite Stabilizer Sled from Steadicam could certainly be used for more than just that. However, if you do work in broadcast and are looking for a new, lightweight stabilization system, this one will be no slouch, as it’s set to come equipped with two adjustable V-mount battery plates that can be pivoted and shifted around for optimal placement—giving users plenty of flexibility in terms of balance and motion. This new Stabilizer Sled will also feature a rigid top stage that should help reduce vibration transfer, increasing 30 lb load capacity and stability. It will also have some helpful fine-adjust controls on the side of the stage that should further help it be ready for quick, intuitive on-the-fly adjustments. The company also reports that this Elite version will come with an integrated 3-axis Volt gimbal and pan assistance to help users maintain their horizon line. Price and Availability The new Steadicam Elite Stabilizer Sled will be available with selectable 12V and 24V power distribution options, supported by the sled without requiring external adapters. items.title: 3 Words That Should Be on the First Page of Your Script
items.summary: I wanted to write about something ridiculous today. So I legit was like, what are three words that I think would stand out on the opening page of a script and get me to lean in? What started as a new exercise for me quickly became this post. Before you write an email to me in anger, I want to tell you that this is not prescriptive. Do whatever you need to do, write whatever you want. But this was a fun way to break me out of my normalcy and try to do something unique on the opening page of my script. Let's have some fun. 1. "EXCEPT" Okay, this was one I was playing with this morning. You want the opening page to set expectations: genre, protagonist, and tone. But what if you started on a subversion? Starting a script with an exception instantly creates conflict, whether on the page or in the reader's mind. You can force the reader to ask a question. If everything in the world functions one way except for this one person, place, or rule, the story has already begun. Let's expand on that idea. How to use it: Put it right in your opening action description or voiceover to disrupt the status quo in sentence one. Example: Everyone in Suburbia Heights cleans their gutter on Sunday morning. Except Arthur. Arthur spends Sunday mornings throwing rock salt at the mailman. See how that shows us who Arthur is right away? We see this is the exception to a rule, the one person who rebels, and we also see he's kind of a nutty guy, too. 2. "SUDDENLY" I probably overuse this word in my writing, but why not add one more on the first page just to set the reader up for a few others in big moments along the way? Seriously though, when placed intentionally, a word like "suddenly" acts as a sudden jolt to the reader's pulse. It signals the exact moment the normal world collapses and something exciting steps in. Page one needs energy. This word provides it. items.title: The Best Opening Scenes in War Movie History
items.summary: We all know that opening scenes are all about setting the tone for the movie, but if you're strapping in for a war film, how can you set the genre while also delivering something more surprising than just a battle? We already know that when we're watching one of these kinds of films, the stakes are inherently life-and-death. Today, I want to talk about how the best opening scenes in war movie history use that to their advantage, while also finding a way to set the theme right from the start. Let's dive in. 1. Apocalypse Now (1979): The Art of the Psychological Dissolve - YouTube www.youtube.com The opening of this movie functions as a Doors music video juxtaposed against the horror of Vietnam. You get the music, the sound of the helicopters, the exploding jungle, and suddenly you're inside Francis Ford Coppola's madness. He and legendary sound designer Walter Murch collaborated to deliver one of the most iconic openings in cinematic history. The Technique: Slow-motion dissolves overlay a line of peaceful palm trees and a thumping helicopter blade, taking us to an overhead fan beating down hot air on the ghostly, upside-down face of Captain Willard (Martin Sheen). We're right inside this guy's mind, and we can see the toll war has already taken on him. And it's going to ask for more. The Sound Design: Murch was actually the first person credited as a sound designer ever for this movie. He matched the rhythmic whirp-whirp of helicopter blades to the sound of a ceiling fan in Willard’s Saigon hotel room. It set the existential tone right away without needing any words. Filmmaking Lesson: You don't need a multi-million-dollar explosion to convey internal chaos. Sure, we have one here, but the real tension is bringing us into Sheen's frame of mind and thenhis stupoor of drinking and thrashing. items.title: Blackmagic Design Adds New Capture and Playback Support With Desktop Video 16.3 Update
items.summary: Another Blackmagic Design firmware update is out, this time with the latest Desktop Video update (version 16.3), focused on adding improvements for the DeckLink 8K Pro Mini, as well as other top models in this space. If you’re currently using Blackmagic Design’s low-profile, 8-lane PCIe Gen2 digital cinema capture and playback card, or interested in adding it to your workflows, here’s what you need to know about this latest update and what it’s set to add with new support for HANC capture and playback. Blackmagic Design Desktop Video Update While this isn’t a major Desktop Video update from Blackmagic Design, it is notable for those who use or are interested in a few specific products. Namely, the DeckLink 8K Pro Mini, the DeckLink 8K Pro G2, and the UltraStudio Express Monitor 3G, as all three of these products are set to get improvements. However, while the latter two are mostly just getting minor bug fixes, the DeckLink 8K Pro Mini is set to get the biggest boost with new support for capturing and playing back horizontal ancillary data, as well as improved ancillary data capture. This should be quite welcome news for anyone using this popular low-profile 8-lane PCIe Gen2 digital cinema capture and playback card, which has a lot of appeal thanks to its four bidirectional 12G-SDI micro-BNC connectors, which allow it to be a nice option for accepting resolutions from SD, DCI 4K (4096 x 2160), and DCI 8K at up to 60 fps. Desktop Video Update 16.3 Here’s the full list of everything in Desktop Video 16.3: New feature on DeckLink 8K Pro Mini: Add support for HANC capture and playback. Bug fix on DeckLink 8K Pro G2: Fix a bug preventing capture of some HANC packets in 6G and 12G modes. Bug fix for UltraStudio Express Monitor 3G: Fix intermittent playback issue in 1080p23.98 and 1080p29.97 formats. And here’s the full breakdown of what models are currently supported for this update: DeckLink Duo 2 DeckLink Quad 2 DeckLink Quad HDMI Recorder DeckLink 8K Pro G2 DeckLink 4K

items.title: The Most Memorable Movie Friendships
items.summary: There are a few shortcuts we can use as filmmakers to quickly gain audience buy-in, and telling a story about friendship is one method. It can be the driving force of a narrative regardless of genre and often is. Or it can just add emotional texture. Either way, you can hang a lot on friendships, whether they're just developing or long-established, because of what it reveals about characters and backstories. Buddy comedies, romance films, enemies-to-friends tales—so many stories rely on characters having this most fundamental relationship. You can build an entire universe around friendship. Today we're taking a look at some of the most iconic movie friendships and what they can teach us. Come on, buddy! - YouTube www.youtube.com Sam and Frodo in The Lord of the Rings Trust me, you could pick almost any duo from Peter Jackson's trilogy as an example of strong friendship. Merry and Pippin, Legolas and Gimli... Saruman and Wormtongue. But the most iconic pair has to be Sam (Sean Astin) and Frodo (Elijah Wood), the Hobbits who saved Middle-earth. Astin told The Wrap that the emotional scene when Sam runs after Frodo at the end of The Fellowship of the Ring wasn't even in the original script. "When Frodo and Sam go off on their own at the end of the first film, that scene wasn't written until well into the production. Like well, well, well into the production. And Peter Jackson, Fran Walsh and Philippa Boyens wanted Elijah [Wood] and I to come and have a meeting with them, and we were like, 'Well, this is new.'" What emerged from that scene was the beginning of a brotherly devotion between the pair. If you're finding a friendship, maybe the biggest moments come out of rewrites when you're already shooting. Jackson did this often as he was cutting and keeping from J.R.R. items.title: The 2008 Movie That Made Timothée Chalamet Want to Act
items.summary: Can you remember the movie that made you want to work in film? That memory is a little hazy for me. I had a few distinct childhood periods of hyperfixation that certainly contributed, including a paleontology phase inspired by Jurassic Park and a space obsession triggered by Apollo 13 and Star Wars. Soon I had stolen my family's camera and was making videos whenever I could wrangle my cousins as crew. It's always interesting to see those inspiration points in other storytellers, too. What about Timothée Chalamet? In 2024, the actor gave an interview to The New York Times alongside Denis Villeneuve in which they discussed the making of Dune: Part Two. During the discussion, he revealed the movie that made him want to be an actor was Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight. He would have been 12 years old at the time. It's safe to call this a formative experience for him. Isn't it wild how some moving images on a screen can change a person's life? We want to look at that phenomenon today. What did Chalamet see in the film, and what can filmmakers learn? - YouTube www.youtube.com Why the Screening Changed Everything Chalamet was asked about whether he'd been offered superhero roles, which the reporter noted had started to fizzle out in the zeitgeist. "Well, Leonardo DiCaprio said to me, 'No superhero movies, no hard drugs,'" he replied. "Which I thought was very good." Villeneuve asked which particular bit of advice he was following. "I follow them both!" he said. "But the movie that made me want to act is a superhero movie, The Dark Knight. If the script was great, if the director was great, I'd have to consider it." This isn't the first time Chalamet has mentioned the movie's impact on him. In 2018, he received the Best Actor award at the New York Film Critics Circle Awards for Call Me by Your Name. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: 'The Last Samurai' Line That Quietly Defined Purpose
items.summary: Tom Cruise is such a massive star that I don't feell ike he has any forgotten hits, but I was scrolling my library last week and pulled out The Last Samurai. I mean, when was the last time you watched this movie? It's Tom Cruise and Ken Watanabe in an Ed Zwick epic that's about not only the East meeting the West but overcoming your own personal demons to be a part of something bigger than yourself and taking your place in history, dying for what you believe is right. One of the most powerful scenes in the movie is not a battle but a quiet conversation about fate. Let's dive in. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Scene in Question Okay, this movie is about Tom Cruise playing a Civil War and American Indian Wars veteran who has PTSD and is now living in Japan. He's hired to join the Imperial Japanese Army to train its recruits. The recruits are not good, and they all get forced into battle too early. In that fight, Captain Nathan Algren (Tom Cruise) is captured and spared by samurai leader Moritsugu Katsumoto (Ken Watanabe). Stripped of alcohol and forced out of his downward spiral, Algren now becomes a member of the samurai forces he was hired to destroy. These two men form a bond as Algren slowly comes to see the other side. Katsumoto doesn't interrogate Algren about military tactics; instead, he asks about his nightmares, his history, and his soul. Algren sees human existence as a series of chaotic, regret-filled accidents that have driven him across the globe, away from his sins. But Katsumoto views every trauma as a way to get to another destination that might be better. These tête-à-têtes between the men carry the entire middle of the movie, as they then plan to fight back against the Imperial Forces, who want to destroy the samurai villages.
